en: From the *New Compilation of the Postscript on Forest Seclusion*, in praise of the portrait of Śākyamuni’s departure from the mountains:
"Qin Yue-ren, in the art of medicine, could discern life and death by a mere glance; Old Pan, in the art of ink, could discern its refinement by touch."
Roughly speaking, this is because its subtle essence that has not been transmitted leaves no ground for expressing it through speech or silence. The Duke Wenzhong of Ouyang said:
"Although the names of the calligraphers of the *Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching* in small characters are not recorded, none but Wang Xizhi could have produced such a work.
I examined the image of Śākyamuni Buddha Emerging from the Mountains preserved by the family of Qian Yue; although the name of the artist is not mentioned, it is none other than [Wang Xizhi].
Daozi was unable to create it, for the intent of his brushstrokes was so profoundly manifest. Lü Dao’s character was exceedingly lofty;
following his consumption of iron and blood, this image was commissioned through the power of his sincere faith and profound reverence. It is by no means a trivial matter.
With hands joined and head bowed in prostration, I offer this eulogy: [Insert Eulogy Here]
The flavor of the entire great ocean is contained within a single drop; the bodies filling the entire dharma-realm are accommodated within a speck of dust.

If one pauses to reflect, even the throne of King Dīpaṃkara cannot enter the chamber of Vaiśālī; yet when one withdraws the mind in concentration, the gate of Maitreya opens at a mere snap of the fingers.
It was our ancestral patriarch, Śākyamuni Bhikṣu, who first emerged from the Snowy Mountains and manifested this very image. With hundreds and thousands...

With bodies as numerous as hundreds of millions of motes of dust and the ninety-seven marks of a Great Man, he suddenly entered the Samādhi of the Brush-tip and conjured this upon a single sheet of paper:
hands hanging down, feet bare, a conch-shell curl atop his head, and a silken strand at his jaw. Transcendent, serene, and profound, he has emerged from the delusions of the three realms;
like a vast springtime wind resting upon a slender branch, or like the cool moon reflected in a basin of water, he is carved and chiseled from ice.
I, Xue, have composed these verses of praise. May Master Guankongluo Meng store them away securely.
The monk Zijiong, using fine hair as a slender brush, made its point as sharp as a rhinoceros horn; when he applied it to paper, his movement of the elbow was as swift as the wind.

Rain. He inscribed the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* within a circular mandala measuring one chi and two cun. Viewed from afar, it appeared perfectly round, like a pearl amidst thin mist; yet upon closer inspection, the arrangement of the characters was as intricate as a person combing their hair into a swirling chignon.

Were it not for a subtle and refined power of contemplation, how could such a feat have been achieved? In praise of this, he wrote: The golden script, set within a jade-like circle, Appears from afar like a pearl in the morning mist. Yet when viewed closely, the characters are laid out Like braided locks of hair fashioned into a coiled chignon.
Were it not for a mind of subtle and profound power, How could such a marvel have been attained?
In the past, there was a son of the Buddha with sharp and keen faculties, who was able to perceive that emptiness is itself form.

Wishing to manifest the inconceivable nature of emptiness and form, he inscribed these Vajra verses upon the sky. To this day, when wind and rain sweep across the plains, woodcutters gather beneath them;
only then do they realize that the fleshly eye cannot see. It is like the taste of salt within water—only those on the Path, such as Master Qiong, can perceive it.

My contemplation is exquisite and unique; I am able to perceive that the nature of form is itself emptiness. Beholding this slender tube as vast as a ridgepole, my brush sweeps across it like a carriage traversing a nine-lane highway.
Thus, within a ringed wheel of but a few inches, the entire body of vast and expansive discourse is fully contained.
To the people of the world, it may be seen but cannot be read—just as an infant gazes at honey on a precipice. I, however, am able to realize and enter into this sutra from its very beginning.

The three Dharma-gates that are good in the middle and at the end: suddenly taking up the brush, it is like water poured from a high roof; no longer do active mental states give rise to inverted conceptions.

It is like the contemplation of form and emptiness entering all objects, or like the skilled butcher’s blade gliding through the joints of an ox without encountering solid flesh. May I exhaustively uphold this Dharma to bestow upon all sentient beings;
may those with most subtle wisdom likewise realize it together with me.
**Eulogy for the Six Patriarchs, with Preface** After I had been exiled to the sea for three years, I returned and took up residence at Shimen Temple in Junzhou.

Grieving for the desolation of the monastic groves and reflecting upon the lofty character of our patriarchs, I could not help but shed tears. Thus, I composed this eulogy for the portraits of the six patriarchs.
This was entrusted to Chan Master Zhao Mo, to reveal his resolve:

"Delusive thoughts have no inherent nature; they are realized as the non-extinction of sensation. This is what the former sages knew, transmitted from hand to hand like the blooming of wind-blown flowers."
The vessel-world is defined by form; when the frost and dew cause the fruit to ripen, the Prince is born. He upholds the Buddha-vehicle and points to the essence of the mind;

he merely negates what is false, rather than asserting what is true. When an infant seeks an object, his intention is correct though his speech is partial; this occurs within the state of "da" and "o."
Words and meaning are both discarded.
Like the morning dew upon a mountain peak, his divine radiance ascends at night; he is fit to receive the single transmission and shoulder the supreme vehicle, seeking the mind for himself.

He saw no place of refuge; it was like looking at a spinning wheel, seeking its breaks and continuities. He used the prison to eliminate the gaps between [birth and death], and by walking upon emaciation he came to know fullness.
In brothels and wine shops, he exhausted all worldly mechanisms. Like cutting off his own arm in the snow, he vowed to prolong the Buddha’s life. His descendants hear this now.

With bristling hair and palms pressed together, one beholds the darkness and obscurity of the six realms; yet, unimpeded by this, one realizes the clarity and purity that does not deviate by even a hair’s breadth. Having realized the extinction of ambrosia, there remains only the bare skull.

He specifically avoided using his surname and given name; he transcended perceptions and rose above worldly emotions. Desiring to exhaust all worldly burdens, he lived in seclusion by streams, by the sea, and among the mountains.

Wearing hempen robes and wind-hats, he moved back and forth with ease. Clad in coarse cloth yet harboring precious gems within, he refined his sincerity to its ultimate point. Having renounced both body and fame, he left no tomb or grave for future generations.
It is as if there were no one who understood.

At the foot of Mount Pòtóu, dragons and elephants thronged together; the robe was entrusted to a child, and the Way was transmitted to a lazy monk. Thus, things have come to such a state of contradiction.

He sought people for the sake of the Dharma; when a divine letter arrived at his door, he lay prostrate and did not answer it. He contemplated all sentient beings who were like those grasping at wind or catching shadows;
though they had been treated by the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), they still had not awakened. The Master smiled and said: "Why must you be so deluded? Simply do not insist on giving them names."

Naturally free from illness, one contemplates the preceding and succeeding bodies as two mirrors facing each other on a single surface; these three appear simultaneously, such that what is now is not what was before.

Adding gold makes it yellow; what was wrong in the past is right now. Slander sinks one into the scentless; having already severed birth and death, how could one still be entangled by youth or old age?
When the total mechanism manifests before you, it is luminous and wondrous. Like a night river assisting a boat, I shall now ferry you across. This is the eye within the phrase.
It is like there being milk in water.
It is the wind and the banner that move; the eye merely conceals and protects it. It is not the wind and the banner that move; the mind is what is revealed. This is Caoxi.

This reveals the essential point of definitive resolution. Those who wish to realize it must not let their minds wander; for a moment, gather your thoughts. Wondrously quiescent and luminously clear, this is for your own personal enjoyment;
it is secretly not found on my side. It is like carrying stones to pound grain, or chasing deer and hares after they have already fled—it is like the emptiness within a mirror.
Seeking it through desire, there is no path.
The *Praise of the Portrait of the Mahāsattva Zao Bo*, with Preface:

The profound and mysterious depths of the *Yi* cannot be grasped through mere rational meaning; therefore, the hexagram judgments (*tuan*) and images (*xiang*) were established to exhaust its purport. The essence of the mind...
The subtle cannot be transmitted through words; therefore, phenomena are pointed out to demonstrate its wondrousness. Only the Great Being Zao Bo has deeply entered this gate of samādhi.
With the utmost reverence, I prostrate myself and offer this eulogy:
His mustache and eyebrows were like a painting; he was tall and handsome. His spirit and demeanor were as majestic as the autumn air. Throughout his life, he took his rest in the northeast.
Amidst the toil of the mundane world, he remained tranquil and still. He walked with bare feet and disheveled robes, carefree and unhurried.

Within the functioning of wisdom upon wisdom, he never deviated from its essence. Born into a royal family, he attained sovereign mastery. His lifespan cannot be recorded, for it transcends beginning and end. Even tigers obeyed his commands.
The mind and its objects are empty; with women as companions, one abandons both hatred and love. The transmission of the mind through the crown and kerchief is the mundane truth;

the demonstration of the Dharma through the various quarters is the principle within phenomena. Using only jujube and *bō* fruit to offer to the alms bowl, I have come to Jambudvīpa not for the sake of taste.
Natural radiance arises from my teeth and gums; the verses and compositions I speak are all of true meaning. O Son of the Buddha, I grant you this manifest decision. One.

A single word is sufficient to transcend the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Following ignorance gives rise to all states of existence (*bhava*); by not following it, one leaves all states of existence behind.

Just as the cream of the noble ones arises from the milk of ordinary beings, this occurs solely through the contemplation of ethical discipline (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).

This is called the great being’s compassion of identical essence, which causes me to suddenly enter into all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and perform great Buddha-works throughout all dust-motes and lands, contained within the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha*).
Reining in my chariot, I take emptiness as my seat and pay homage to the ten bodies [of the Buddha]. Taking aspiration as my tongue, I speak this verse:
it is like describing boundless springtime with flowers, or like describing the taste of the great ocean with a single drop. I bow my head to the wondrous lotus of the world;
may I always aspire to remain pure and emerge from the mire.
Eulogy and Preface for the Venerable Baizhang Dazhi Chan Master Chan Master Mazu Daoci had already passed away and was interred at Shimen in Haihun.

The Master [Baizhang] resided beside it for a long time, and those seeking him as a disciple increased daily. Thereupon, weary of the mountain's shallowness, he followed the Feng River upstream until he reached...
Beneath the Peak of the Chariot Wheel (Che-lun-feng), he and Xi-yun Wei-zheng cultivated the land with fire and the blade to provide for their sustenance, and thus established a Dharma assembly.
In the spring of the fourth year of the Chongning era, I went into the mountains to behold his portrait.

Although his body appeared as withered as ice and aged by snow, seemingly unable to support its own weight, his spirit was lofty and his countenance transcendent, as if he had not yet passed into the world. I reverently prostrated myself and composed this eulogy: [The eulogy follows.]
To answer with reality, emptiness could be blue or yellow. To seek the Way with the mind causes the spirit to fall into yin and yang. Yin and yang cannot be fathomed;
when one transcends and disregards the realm of yin, even empty space is inexhaustible. Cause and effect are not obscure: I possess the great capacity, and the Buddha has no secret words.
Like a lion king, he sat exposed upon the open ground; his words, which accorded with the nature of reality, followed him wherever he went like a forest.

As if using a skillful finger to produce harmonious and elegant sounds, he moved in accordance with the waves of the world. He lived to the age of ninety-two, upheld the heart-essence of the Dharma, and was posthumously titled "The Great Wise One" (Dazhi).

Eulogy for Yun’an Zhen: Yun’an emerged from the lineage of Huanglong. He was the ninth-generation descendant of Linji. His spiritual nature was exceptionally eminent and his realization vast and profound.

In pointing out the essentials of the mind, his eloquence was like that of Caoqi; in discerning and resolving the vehicles of the teachings, his discourse was like that of Zhaobo. His literary compositions were likewise unsurpassed.
The verses were composed in a style like that of Master Zhigong, while his step-by-step realization of the truth was as refined as that of Master Yongjia.

He retired to Yun’an at the age of over seventy; with all illusions extinguished, his wisdom-light was perfectly round and complete. One can thus imagine the enduring influence of his remaining legacy.
The disciple Dehong respectfully prostrates himself with his head to the ground and offers this eulogy:

Within the realm of self-abiding, the seeing and the objects of seeing are like the subject and object in a dream, or like the center and periphery of honey; only those who possess the correct eye can perceive them as such.
Entering this samādhi is like a wondrous lotus flower emerging from the ocean of dependent origination.

The living intent of the Patriarchs and the secret mechanism of the Tathāgata accomplish sentient beings like the soaring of the kunpeng bird, causing them to transform themselves spontaneously without awakening through another; they stand out preeminent within the groves of the sangha.
His radiance shone upon the Buddhas and Patriarchs. He passed away in the region of Shanxi and was reborn in Jiangnan. Amidst the darkness, the five colors appeared;
throughout the realm, Yun’an became renowned.
This is the "Inscription for the Mingji Shrine" composed by Wang Jian Boqiang of Taiyuan—a son of the eminent official Duke Hui and a son-in-law of the Imperial Uncle Prince Jia. At that time—

In his prime, he was able to resign his official post to study the Way. Upon reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* to the passage, "When the remaining dust has been cleared away, the various studies reach their ultimate clarity, which is precisely the Tathāgata," he sighed and said, "This is the instruction of the Tathāgata and my own aspiration.

He wished to name his study hall "Ultimate Clarity" (*Mingji*) and requested an inscription from me. The inscription reads: In his prime, he was able to resign his official post to study the Way. Upon reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* to the passage, "When the remaining dust has been cleared away, the various studies reach their ultimate clarity, which is precisely the Tathāgata," he sighed and said, "This is the instruction of the Tathāgata and my own aspiration.
He wished to name his study hall "Ultimate Clarity" (*Mingji*) and requested an inscription from me. The inscription reads: [The remainder of the inscription follows.]

Seeking that which already exists is the confinement of ignorance; to be startled and amazed upon attaining it is the fault of turbid wisdom. When turbidity clears and darkness is transparent, self-awakening is accomplished.
It is like the pupil of the eye, which does not admit even a single speck of dust; the opening of the eyelids is likened to birth, and the arising of clarity depends upon the faculties.

Closing one's eyelashes is like death; yet even in darkness, it cannot cause blindness. The True Compassion of the Holy Master has opened this wondrous gate. To look askance and refuse to enter—how could such a person know gratitude?
Within the empty chamber stands a simple square bed; there one walks in meditation or sits in repose, with lamps burning at dawn and incense wafting at dusk.
Do not allow perverse thoughts to obscure the eternally quiescent light.
[This concludes] the verses of the *Sūtra of the Flower Garland* in small characters, together with its preface.
Bees’ hives are formed within the rafters, their cells secured by resin; magpies’ nests are built at the treetops, accumulated over a hundred days.
It was accomplished later. How could that assembly have known it? Yet, the subtlety of its execution and the merit of its accumulation were like the divine mastery of an artisan.

For although its inconceivable power—its numinous clarity and vast penetration—is obscured even amidst the slightest fluttering of movement, it is fully perfected without deviating by so much as a hair’s breadth;
how much more so for that which stands preeminent above all things, responding to phenomena and capable of speech?

In the past, there was a Brahman monk who came from the Five Indies. Upon seeing the grandeur and splendor of the Jin palace, he sighed and said, "How is this different from the Inner Court of Tuṣita?
That was produced by the power of spiritual cultivation, whereas this is merely the result of karmic force. I have often laughed at him.
How could one know that this wondrous power of mine gives birth to the Great Void and accommodates the entire universe?

What need is there to speak of palatial towers and pavilions in heaven or among men? The Dharma Master Sengqi, pitying the confinement of the world, acted according to people's desires and transcribed the *Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra* into bound volumes.
Its lightness and subtlety allow it to be placed upon a single palm; when opened—

The interwoven, wriggling lines were like marching ants. Upon close inspection, their horizontal and diagonal, curved and straight, overlapping and inverted turns displayed the utmost subtlety, appearing no different from characters written in large, bold "split-nest" script (*bèikē*). Onlookers crowded the gate, marveling at such an unprecedented sight.
Desiring to praise this merit of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*), he addressed the great assembly and spoke these verses:
I have heard that the Venerable Master Nāgārjuna, an Arhat, once entered the Sāgara Ocean;

there, he could recite from memory at a single glance any subtle verse found among the atoms of the dragon palace. These teachings spread throughout the Five Indias and China, serving as a gateway to nectar for those afflicted by the heat of suffering.
Subsequently, the Daoist practitioner Xi appeared; his vow-power was fierce and sharp, and his contemplation was exceptionally refined, such that he was able [to master] the written volumes.
Between paper and ink, I have written this great sūtra of one hundred thousand verses; reciting it within my snail-shell hut and thatched cottage, it was as clear as if seen in the Dragon Palace.
Those who observe it differ in their spiritual dispositions (*gotra*); according to their inclinations, they each give rise to distinct perceptions.
One must carefully observe that even within a single mote of dust there exists a boundless, wondrous scroll of scripture. Long ago, a wise person shattered this mote of dust into ten...

All that is spoken throughout the worlds is comprised within these two characters. Because they take names as their objects, they are not empty annihilation; because they can be dismantled, they are not substantially real.
To comprehend this wondrous Dharma-gate of two characters is likewise to encompass the ocean of all sūtras.

It is like one who, while lying exhausted for a mere moment, experiences a thousand years within a dream; thus one knows that a single thought-moment encompasses past and present within the realm of true reality. The Dharma...
Thus it is. A single atom is subtle and immeasurable; one should know that every single atom is likewise so.

It is like the bright jewels of Indra’s net: the substance of each jewel is luminous and mutually transparent, such that a single jewel contains all the other jewels of the net, and they all enter into one another simultaneously.
By means of these vajra-words, I shall now destroy those inferior conceptions and cause them to awaken.
This sutra is contained within the very dust; why then should one be startled by its presence in volumes? I address you, O deities of mountains, rivers, and trees:
each of you should recall the power of your original vows. You must vigilantly and courageously provide protection, ensuring that no perverse thoughts may ever cause it harm or decay.

When the Vairambha winds blow upon Mount Sumeru, and the kalpa-fire incinerates the great trichiliocosm, may this sutra be spread throughout all places, so that they may find cool relief and each attain their proper state.
For us, the sons of the Buddha present here, to perform this visualization is called right contemplation.
We prostrate to the Teachers who Subdue the World throughout the ten directions, who serve as witnesses in every land and within every atom of dust.
Eulogy on the Sandalwood Image of Bodhisattva Maitreya,
with Preface The sandalwood image of Bodhisattva Maitreya at Huazang Chan Temple in Jinling possesses a craftsmanship of physical marks and excellence that is the most marvelous in all under heaven.
The divine wonders and spiritual responses of this image are too numerous to be easily counted. It resided in the rear hall of Jingde Temple.
Once, Lord Wang (Wang Anshi) dreamed that the image urgently requested to be moved to another location; upon waking, he forgot the matter. However, he subsequently dreamed again of the same affair.
In the dream, the Lord firmly urged him to remain, whereupon the image wept. When he rose to look at it, there were indeed traces of tears on its face. Thereupon—
Greatly amazed, they immediately welcomed it and enshrined it in the Great Hall of Huazang. Suddenly, Jingde Temple was reduced to ashes overnight. Alas!
When the three calamities envelop the great trichiliocosm and bring about its destruction, how could an image remain long in the world of men?

To suffer such a painful humiliation as this, like a mere child’s play or a narrow and inferior spectacle—is this not because the *dharmapāla* devas, through the spiritual power of the image, [have acted]?
That such auspicious protection occurred was not the intention of the Bodhisattva; this must be clearly distinguished. Bowing my head, I offer this eulogy:
Who has harbored these lofty aspirations, sporting amidst floating bubbles? By the power of illusion, they have carved this sandalwood image.
Sitting thus, his myriad wondrous marks burst forth radiantly amidst a thousand beams of light. A celestial crown binds his deep-blue hair; fine garments are interlaced with flower garlands.
Adorned with various exquisite ornaments, he has become this mass of merit. At that time, the hundreds of millions of beings, moved to the utmost, wailed in grief.

From the towers and pavilions, laughter and conversation emerge; a hundred treasures are gathered in secret protection. It is as if ascending to the Tuṣita Heaven, or as if attending the Dragon Flower Assembly.
Alas! At the end of the Semblance Dharma, the *yujia* bird has become a hundred crows; thorns have grown within the *campaka* grove. Even the dragon deities are moved by sorrow.
The king and his ministers have truly provided external protection; these strange dreams were not of my own making. I pray you push forth the bright moon’s orb to dispel this surging smoke;
I pray you turn back the Purple Gold Mountain and settle it in a cool, refreshing place. Thus, until now, the hundred marks of merit remain solemnly present before gods and men.

The power of his spiritual transformations is indeed unfathomable; gazing upon him with reverence, my tears flow in torrents. As I contemplate the ten directions with clarity, I see that there are truly no external objects apart from the mind.
Thus, one naturally becomes free from both the dependent nature and the imputed nature. That which is currently seen by the eyes is neither existent nor non-existent.

Just as an image appears in a mirror, yet is neither the mirror nor the face, may I enter this samādhi so that the consciousness-mind is spontaneously luminous, performing great Buddha-work throughout the lands of the ten directions.
I prostrate to the Honored One of Great Compassion; please bear witness to these words of mine.
The Fifteenth Patriarch’s True Eulogy, with Preface:
Venerable Kāṇadeva was the fifteenth patriarch. Having transmitted the Buddha’s mind-seal, he remained concerned that sentient beings were unable to believe and accept his words.
He then addressed the image of Maheśvara, saying: "I pray that the Divine One will grant me..."
This ensures that my words are not spoken in vain. Alas! That the Way is difficult to practice is not unique to the present age. I prostrate and offer this praise:
"The stone tiger is drunk with flesh; the wooden horse neighs at night. This samādhi of mine is not known through conscious intellect; it manifests in response to conditions."

It does not fall within the realm of discursive thought; this is the answer regarding the bowl of water. To cast a needle into it is like Zhongni’s performance of the *Shao* music, like Ziqi’s mastery of the zither, or like Xiao He recognizing the man from Huaiyin.
There are no words upon which to rely and no tracks to be sought; yet, it manifests brilliantly before one.
Transmitted from mind to mind, like the eyes of a statue in a cave; I do not presume upon the deity, yet I know the cause through the ears of the pointing tree.
Things and self are as they were before; all that is established is true. Following its wondrous function, one beholds my entire body. I prostrate myself before this True Compassion.
He is the king among the Sangha; like the moon among ten thousand stars, those who behold him feel refreshing coolness.
Yet he still laments that sentient beings do not believe, for this is surely the fault of the blind, not because his light is obscured.
A Eulogy for the Venerable Master Chuyuan Zhen:
I am one who shares the same current as both Jing and Wei. Amidst laughter, I am a soft-natured, slippery fellow. For you, I shall snatch away both person and environment;

amidst the clamor, I employ the clever theft of the "white-handed" thief. Like water washing water, like tower striking tower—ever free and unconstrained, without a fixed pattern—to receive [the seeker].
He obtained the Dharma-lineage of Nanquan as a successor to Zhaozhou.

The true eulogy for Master Zhaomo possesses a discernment like that of Xuansha, yet with a sense of proportion; it has a resonance like that of Muzhou, yet with a spirit of loftiness. In silence, he spoke of the pearl from within himself.
Illuminating the eight wildernesses, his radiance rests upon a single hair; standing alone at Nanrong, he is as majestic as a towering mountain. Linji wished to overturn him but dared not do so;
with a smile, he brandishes his jade whisk, its air like spring. In the solemn stillness of the hall, the heavenly demons weep.
Preface to the Eulogy by Kōshō (Kongsheng):
The monk Shēnxiū of Zhāngnán traveled to the region of Wú, where he discovered this painting amidst the ruins of a crumbling wall.

Having brushed away the dust and grime, its spiritual appearance became serene and profound; it was as if one had attained liberation of mind from the Great Being Vimalakīrti. He then brought it forth to show me.
I offer this eulogy:
With a body of emptiness and stillness, there is no place upon which to rely or dwell, yet he grasps the staff and gourd. With a mind of numinous awareness, it neither scatters nor concentrates.
While handling the palm leaves, one does not abandon sounds and forms; yet one realizes the true emptiness (*śūnyatā*). This accords with my daily life, where subject and object are identical.
In all places, one enters the ocean of Dharma in stillness; like the wind moving through space, there is no obstruction. One need only be liberated from the two attachments.
The Perfectly Accomplished Universal Assembly: One Should Cultivate with Care. Entering this Samādhi.
Eulogy for the Portrait of Master Yongming, with Preface.
Chan Master Yongming Zhijue, by the power of his compassionate vows, manifested birth in China to transmit the Mind-essence of the Buddha and serve the Dharma.
Donor, the family of this scholar named Biancai has gained renown for its erudition; his discourse and utterances are as vast as the mountains and seas.

For more than twenty years, I have fished and hunted among them, and whenever I reached their subtle depths, I was able to discern them—just as the king of geese selects milk from water without leaving anything behind.
Thus, I have often forgotten my own meanness and wished to pursue the master’s transcendent course.
I shall act as your companion to travel through the lands of the ten directions and perform great Buddha-work; it is not yet too late.
Bowing my head, I offer this eulogy:

Within the three realms, there are ten thousand varieties of beauty and ugliness; birth follows the flow while death goes against it, like dreaming at night and imagining by day, revolving without interval.
Sounds passing through walls and windows all depend upon the manas; thus are conceptual proliferations accomplished.

Yet the essence of the manas is without action and without reception, like a flower in the sky—truly non-existent yet appearing to exist. To realize this in a single thought-moment is for the light to penetrate through; such is my vision.
Free from error, this is the core of the mind. The patriarchs and Buddhas extended their hands; who shall now uphold the collapsing order?
Outstanding, eminent, extraordinary, and flourishing—I prostrate before Yongming, like the moon facing the stars and constellations.

Eulogy for the Portrait of Venerable Yongjia, with Preface The Venerable of Yongjia first read the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* and thereby clarified the essential point of the mind. Desiring to establish the fundamental tenets, he traveled to Caoxi to seek certification from the Patriarch;
after staying there for one night, he departed. Consequently, the world has come to know him by the name "Awakened in One Night" (Yisuo Jue). Having read this, I...
Regarding the lyrics of this work, when I examined his actual practice, it was like a ruler meeting its mark or a lock fitting its key; I could not help but set down the scroll and sigh deeply.

I imagine that the man’s character was vast and luminous, standing tall and firm like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high, while viewing the current scholars who are meager, narrow-minded, and swarming about like insects.
From this, one can know the rise and fall of the religious tradition. For this, I offer a eulogy: [Insert Eulogy Here]

The faculty of feeling is without merit; the mental consciousness is without action. Direct perception is perfectly accomplished. Seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving are like a mirror receiving a lamp:

the light neither degrades nor mingles. Like a fierce fire burning, a river rushing swiftly, a mountain wind roaring in rage, or the great earth as a foundation—[all these phenomena arise within the nature of reality].
The same applies to those who lack both knowledge and reflection. This gate of nirvāṇa is like a drum smeared with poison:
when Caoqi strikes it, those who hear it fall prostrate. He hands the mallet to you; all phenomena are startled and shrink away. These words of radiant light are as brilliant as the sun and stars.
The practice of sublime discipline is as pure as jade or ice; only that which is not transmitted accords with emptiness.
When I first studied the Way, it was as if my hands were clenched into fists; later I realized it, and my hands became at ease. At times I employ this to grasp the great trichiliocosm.
Eulogy for the Portrait of Chan Master Qingliang Dafa’yan, with Preface:

In the early years of the Yuánfú era, I arrived at Chéngtiān Monastery in Línchuān. The foundations of the monastery were vast and grand enough to accommodate ten thousand people, yet the dining hall was desolate, with only three or four remaining monks.
Reading an old inscription, I learned that this had been the site of Chan Master Dafa’yan.
This is the original foundation of the Dharma’s opening. Within the walls of the Shadow Hall (Yingtang), a painted image remains;

its divine countenance is serene and profound, its features deep and tranquil, yet its spirit of extraordinary brilliance does not fade. Could it be that the outward manifestation of one who bears the Great Dharma and uplifts the four classes of beings is naturally such as this?
I bow my head and offer this eulogy: [Insert Eulogy Here]
It is not the wind or the banner that moves; it is not the wind or the bell that speaks. Seeing and hearing arise and cease, yet they have no locus whatsoever.

How is this clarified? Because all are equally quiescent. This treasury of radiant light is impartially manifest, yet due to fundamental ignorance, craving, desire, strangeness, and jealousy, it remains obscured.

Like a tertian malaria, one must protect oneself from pain. One who is able to comprehend this is identical to original enlightenment. Thus, following conditions as they arise, dwell in leisure and stillness;
let all things remain as they were. With the body free from defilement, act as a model for others—this is the verse of the precipice.
It must not be violated or desecrated, for it is like a great mass of fire.
This is the eulogy and preface for the portrait of Chan Master Yunmen, preserved in the home of the Duke of Zheng, Fu. The monk Yuanjing copied it from the original, which is kept in the collection.
At Mount Jiangshan, in the sixth month of the third year of the Daguan era, I was fortunate enough to pay my respects and behold it. Bowing my head, I composed this eulogy:
"The floodwaters surge to the heavens, yet you stand firm like a mountain. Towering ten thousand fathoms high, you stem the wild waves; one may gaze upon you and be turned back."

He is ungraspable and beyond reach. With a skull like rhinoceros hide and eyes like a tiger’s, his beautiful beard encircles his jaw. His words are like clouds and his mental faculty is like lightning;

his tongue is a thunderbolt that causes heterodox sects to fall and demons’ hearts to shatter. In an instant, all becomes clear and bright—a radiant breeze and a moon in a cloudless sky—while the donkeys and mules of the monastic forests are left behind.
Trampling upon dragons and elephants, he cannot be bound or tethered. His transcendent spirit soars beyond; I could not save him. The great earth appears suddenly as waves;
the clear mechanism [of awakening] passes through his palms.
In the eulogy for the portrait of Chan Master Xuansha Shibei:
"To have mastery at the gateway of the faculties is to perceive phenomena outside the mind; to shift the pivot in the midst of application is to have an answer when questioned."
Questions and answers fly back and forth; one gropes for the Great Way. Mind and phenomena stand in opposition; True Suchness is shattered.
How extraordinary is this old man! He transcends both paths. Before the deceased monk, the waves fully reveal the water; at the tiger’s whiskers, the light spontaneously illuminates the pearl.
The patch-robed monk does not understand; he is like one looking down a well at a donkey.

[The Master] reverently enshrines an image of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara with forty-two arms—whom the Great Compassionate One praised as being like sandalwood—and protects it as he would his own pupils. He wears it upon his head at all times.
I have practiced the Way. I now transmit it to my friend Li Tianfu. For him, I offer this encomium:
"If your mind has words, withered stumps become ghosts; if your mind does not arise, a skull is but water. Thus one knows that deluded perceptions are empty."
One dharma becomes two; it is profoundly still and perfectly luminous. Though there are hundreds of thousands, they are but one.

I bow my head to the Great Being, whose form manifests in response to things, appearing according to their scale, like a valley responding to a sound. With a thousand arms he grasps and holds; with a thousand eyes he observes and illuminates—because he is without mind.
The enjoyment [of this image] is exquisite in every respect, like the vernal season when the essence is hidden within the floral body, yet revealed through its branches and leaves.

Its spiritual presence is manifested in the density and spacing [of its features]; it is solely this auspicious sign: the forty-two arms do not exceed the span of a single inch, and all adornments are perfectly complete.

The pure jewel-eyes are sometimes compassionate and sometimes majestic; as if about to lift their feet, lotus wheels support them. Between the blue spirals of the hair, the countenances of Buddhas appear with solemn dignity.

Like the *jiaomi* insect that nests within the eye of a mosquito, hidden among the stones yet emerging from the shells of oysters and clams, I employ unimpeded compassion that makes no distinction between the pure and the turbid.

I observe that the spiritual dispositions (*gotra*) of those in China are sharp and keen; by means of the wisdom derived from hearing, they shall enter the stage of the extinction of ambrosia (*amṛta*).
May you bestow your grace upon me. May my obstructions be exhausted and my mind opened, so that I may possess unimpeded eloquence like Avalokiteśvara.
When I recited these verses, the myriad phenomena joined their palms in reverence. Why is it unimpeded? Because striking emptiness produces resonance.

Master Yuan’s eulogy: For ten years he accumulated the greenery while standing in attendance; he learned to keep his eyes askance and his nose straight. Throughout his life, he suppressed the monastic community with his presence;
when questioned on the left side, he listened from behind. Master Yiguan deeply concealed his thunderous tongue, yet let the myriad phenomena speak for themselves. Beyond all negations—*babei*.
The four propositions have no place to perch; solitary wind illuminates the multitude like the moon among the stars.
This is the Inscription for the Myeongbae Hermitage, with Preface.

My karmic ties to this world are deep and heavy, and I have long been bound by the constraints of past habits. I am fond of discussing the rise and fall, right and wrong, success and failure of antiquity and the present. [I have] interacted...
Many people traveled about and criticized him for this. Only Chen Yingzhong said, "This does not at all hinder one's progress on the Way;

it is like smoke and clouds over mountains and rivers, or the flowering and lush growth of plants and trees—what we call 'exquisite refinement' and 'diligent cultivation. I knew in my heart that he was joking, yet he did not cease his practice.
In the spring of the first year of the Daguan era, he built a hermitage in Linchuan and named it "Clear and Bright" (Mingbai).
I wished to govern my own afflictions. Upon hearing of this, Yingzhong sent me a verse, saying:

"Not occupying the seat of Vaiśālī within the hermitage, Yet permitted to question the Dharma at Vulture Peak— If one claims that worldly hatred and love have thus ended, Who would be angry when one frowns and leaves the assembly?
Thereupon, the dykes were suddenly breached; furthermore, he spoke much more in this vein. However, in the end, it was precisely because of this that he incurred blame.
Having emerged from nine deaths and barely surviving, I lament that my consciousness was unaware of the subtle and that the Way could not overcome habitual tendencies.
Thus, I have gathered back my soul and spirit and restored my original resolve, composing this inscription for it: [The Inscription] says:
The thunder rolls; ten thousand lands awaken in spring morning. Those who hear it do not speak of it; their minds attain the realization. Leaves fall as the frost clears;
waters recede and the sand remains. Suddenly there is a great commotion, and those who hear it are struck with awe. This union with the wondrous daily functioning is like the thunder of spring.

Turning my back on awakening and the weariness of worldly toil, like a winter thunderclap, I have ceased all myriad affairs. Following conditions with relaxed ease, I am even devoid of cognitive awareness;
how could there be any inverted perceptions? Ever contemplating this kindness, I savor its profound meaning. Withdrawing my body into a single hut, I sleep and rise according to the seasons.
Speech and silence are not obscured; there is not even a hair’s breadth of deviation. Amidst the entanglement of obscurity, one manifests clarity; following sincerity, one attains excellence.
The Inscription for the Bell of Extended Blessings, with Preface.

Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, having relied upon the supernatural power of Master Bao, beheld the景象 (manifestations) of the hells. He asked, "How may these be saved? Master Bao replied: *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly after the dialogue regarding the hells. The full inscription would continue with the specific merits and dedication of the bell.*
The fixed karma of sentient beings cannot be extinguished immediately; they merely find their suffering briefly relieved upon hearing the sound of the bell.
Emperor Wu thereupon issued an edict to all Buddhist temples that the striking of the bell must be slow and drawn out, intending thereby to allow the suffering to linger and subside.
Li Feng and his younger brother [Name] have offered a great bell to Yanfu Monastery, wishing to provide spiritual support for the longevity of their mother, Lady [Name].

May you be blessed and have your past obstacles cleared away. I believe you have understood how to apply your efforts. When Xu Xun of the Jin dynasty ascended to the realm of the immortals in broad daylight, a celestial decree stated:
"We remit your offense of failing to serve your ancestors; we commend your merit in dispensing medicine and chanting incantations over water.

Indeed, dispensing medicine and chanting incantations over water are means to liberate people from suffering. Cui Youfu of the Tang dynasty was originally noble and long-lived, yet he fell ill due to indulging his passions.
To execute, imprison, or fail to release others leads to a short life. Imprisonment and execution place people in suffering. Alas! Life has no fixed form;
it increases when one liberates others from suffering and diminishes when one places them in suffering. Now, the merit and utility of a bell are vast and manifest;
if it is used for giving, the transgressions of a certain person will be extinguished and their life extended. This is the principle.
This is indeed so. For it, I have composed this inscription:
"The great dream of sentient beings busies them with black karma; A clear chime strikes, and their eyes are opened. How could I dare to speak exhaustively of the greatness of this merit?

I pray that my compassionate mother may be freed from the knots of obstruction. Just as sound passes through a wall, she shall immediately transcend [suffering]. How filial are you, elder and younger brothers! But...
Yongyi, relying on the power of the Buddha and others with such piercing urgency, was like one clutching a borrowed object or grasping a scroll of scripture,
praying that his compassionate mother might live as long as spring and endure like a bell constantly struck without end. In the fifth month of summer in the Jiawu year of the Zhenghe era,
Ganlu Mie composed this inscription for him.
Eulogy on the Sandalwood White-Robed Avalokiteśvara Image, with Preface.
This image of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara was enshrined by the monk Yuànjiàn of Sīzhōu Yùán at Tàipíng Sì in Jūn Prefecture.
It was most compassionate, majestic, exquisite, and wondrously sublime, just as that which was seen at Upper Tianzhu.

[The author] asked, "How did you obtain it? Jie replied, "Initially, a guest boat brought it here. It was passed down through several families; whenever a family received it, calamity would soon follow and they would perish.
Everyone was so afraid that they dared not welcome it. Only I welcomed and served it, and no harm befell me. [The author] said, "In the past, Mañjuśrī appeared on Mount Lu..."
The image of Mañjuśrī was unwilling to remain at Hanxi, yet joyfully followed Master Huiyuan back to Donglin.

The Maitreya image of Jinling was unwilling to remain at Jingde Temple, yet appeared in a dream to Prince Xiao Zixian requesting to dwell at Huazang. Now this present image has alone taken up residence in the mirror;
these are all signs of a profound karmic affinity with the Bodhisattva. Otherwise, how could the sacred mind have such [intentions]?
Is it that which one discriminates and then avoids or pursues? For this, I offer a eulogy:

I have heard that when the Bodhisattva was formerly on the causal ground, the Buddha he made offerings to was named Avalokiteśvara. Through hearing, reflection, and cultivation, he awakened to the mind;
by refining the essence of the mind and leaving behind sensory hearing, he attained the Way. Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing cannot be altered, just as, for example, the northwest and...
To the southeast, it is said that hearing may be discarded; this leaves people bewildered and causes them to fall into the net of doubt.

Dragons originally have no ears and hear with their spirit; snakes also have no ears and hear with their eyes; oxen have no ears and therefore hear with their noses; ants have no ears and hear with their bodies.
Such are the various functions of the six sense organs. To claim that hearing may be discarded—how could this possibly be reasonable? Regarding that...

Even amidst heterogeneous, dull, and inferior states, it remains subtle, exquisite, and uninterrupted; how much more so for my sovereign power of compassion and patience—how could unimpeded liberation alone be otherwise?
When a drum and a bell are struck together, their sounds differ; knowing they differ reveals that [the latter] is subject to arising and ceasing.
Yet these two kinds of sounds do not intermingle; they are the simultaneously quiescent Dharma.
I bow my head to the mass of pure wisdom and merit, the vast and magnificent ocean of compassionate vows.

Pitying me, whose power of mental clarity is insufficient, whose seeds of affliction manifest as active conduct from time to time—like a person who becomes intoxicated by wine and, upon being warned against drinking, immediately encounters fine liquor again—I pray that you extinguish my delusions.

May the darkness of ignorance be dispelled; may we obtain the treasury of eloquence and wisdom. May we sport through the lands as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions, bestowing fearlessness and benefiting sentient beings.
All who possess a mind capable of hearing this shall together enter the ocean of the Samādhi of Perfect Penetration.
A Verse in Praise of Zhao Mo: The patch-robed monk has no place to grope;
The painter strikes the mark with every brushstroke. This mountain monk’s drunken eyes cannot rely on them;
I entrust them to the multitude for their critique. If it is like this, kill Lingyuan; If it is not like this, burn the hanging scroll.

Eulogy for the Portrait of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, with Preface On the evening of the *wùzǐ* day of the second month in the spring of the fourth year of the Daguān era, the sick bhikṣu Huìhóng lay prostrate in fetters.
He dreamed that he arrived at a certain place where the courtyard and halls were silent and still. A monk led him into a private chamber and raised a candle.
He saw on the wall an image of the Bodhisattva Bao Gong of Mount Zhong. His heart was filled with joy at the desire to possess it, and the image suddenly fell into his hands.
As he unfolded it to examine it further, it had transformed into the compassionate and majestic form of the Twelve-Faced Avalokiteśvara.
Greatly struck with wonder, he then awoke; it was the third watch. On the day of Jiachen in the third month, Nanzhou Defeng recorded this.
Someone sent a letter inquiring after me, saying, "I have dispatched a monk with my robe and bowl to Lian-shui to paint an image of Avalokiteśvara;

its majesty and adornment are such that no hand in the world could have surpassed it. When Huihong recalled this past event and asked the date the image was sent, he discovered it was the very evening of his dream.
Thereupon, he sighed to himself at how the Bodhisattva, through great compassion and impartial kindness, had shown such pity.
Your compassionate illumination is thus manifest and clear; what kindness or virtue could possibly repay it?

I can do no more than employ pen and tongue, using words and phrases to metaphorically illustrate the depth of the ocean or the brilliance of the sun. I reverently prostrate myself and offer this eulogy:

I prostrate to the Pure and Holy Gate of Ambrosia. Your immeasurable holy bodies pervade all lands as numerous as grains of sand, responding to whatever the hearts of sentient beings seek, like the myriad flowers blooming in the springtime.
Because the Western Quarter is a land of austerity and sorrow, you dwell upon Mount Potalaka.
In this realm, the essence of the teaching lies in sound and hearing; therefore, those who invoke your name attain liberation. All sentient beings...

Their murderous intent was rampant; blinded by ignorance, they neither saw nor gave rise to the aspiration for enlightenment. Thus, [the Bodhisattva] manifested within an eagle’s nest and among clams and oysters, and even acted as a painter to depict his own image.
How could a Bodhisattva possess such diverse states of mind? It is all through the power of his compassionate vows.
Who could have conjured, upon the tip of a single hair, this body adorned with a hundred merits? When it stands firm, about to move, a thousand lights gather around it—like a parable.
As if returning from Mount Zijin, his profound stillness desires to glance upon all living beings; it is as if one were about to pluck a blue lotus.
The barbarian slave, King of Water, comes to offer his sincerity. One imagines seeing fine rain and celestial flowers falling;

amidst the heat and affliction of the five turbidities, sentient beings are steamed and boiled by form, desire, craving, and views. Suddenly beholding this mark of the precious moon, all their pores [are refreshed].
Cool and refreshing, these inconceivable merits have been accomplished entirely through the offerings presented by those of superior mind.
May I quickly be perfumed by the incense of wisdom and insight; may I always wear the robe of compassion and patience; may the mountains of demonic obstacles swiftly crumble and split apart;

and may great wisdom constantly manifest before me. With the essence of mind leaving behind all hearing, I shall realize perfect penetration; naturally, when stillness reaches its ultimate limit, the light will penetrate everywhere. I shall—
In concentration, he is like Avalokiteśvara; may the vows of all sentient beings be fulfilled as mine.
Preface to the Inscription for the Amṛta-Extinction Retreat:
In the spring of the fourth year of the Zhenghe era, I returned from overseas and visited Chan Master Fangguang Yu at Mount Heng, where I was lodged.
Below the village of Lingyuan, he named his residence "The Extinction of Ambrosia" (Ganlu Mie). The practitioner Fatai requested an explanation of its meaning.

I said: "The Third Patriarch received the Dharma at Shaolin in the second year of the Tianping era of the Northern Qi dynasty. He lived in seclusion on Mount Wangong for the rest of his life and never spoke of his surname or name.
Dao'an, during the seventh year of the Kaihuang era of Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty, conducted a census of all private [monasteries] throughout the empire."
When the registers of monks and nuns were being verified, Hui’an said, “I originally have no name,” and subsequently withdrew to Mount Song.

That these two great elders loathed the encumbrances of fame and traces, and refined their Way with such single-mindedness, is indeed thus. I truly admire them, and therefore compose this inscription for them, saying: [The Inscription]
I have heard that by consuming ambrosia one attains longevity, yet it is the Dharma of Nirvana that bears this name. To be born from within Nirvana is for the Valley-Spirit not to die;
only the Buddha and the Lord Lao intend this. Originally I was transcendent and unrestrained, but now I am entangled by anxieties and afflictions.
Now I know he has attained liberation. With beard, hair, and *kāṣāya* robes, Xuan’an hid himself on Mount Songshao; Daojian fled in seclusion to Mount Huo. Thus, Juefan grew old upon Mount Heng.
The mountains have lost their solitary loftiness; the jade has forgotten its flawlessness. May his tongue now forthwith blossom forth as a blue lotus.
Six Poems of the Fisherman:
Ten Thousand Returns.

A jade belt and cloud-patterned robe; the child’s head is bare. Having spent a lifetime laughing and swaggering, one knows for what reason—only after returning from ten thousand *li* does one truly dawn.
At dusk, cease all doubt and hesitation. The great trichiliocosm is grasped within the tip of a single hair. You do not know how to plow the fields or measure out the acres;
yet you can face guests and beat the magnificent drum. Suddenly, with Old An, you whisper in the ear, then push him away, saying: "Do not come to block my path to the ball court."
The spirit of a wild crane on the mountain of medicine, the air of a cloud; its imposing aura is like the dawn of a frosty sky.

Having not yet finished reading the remaining sutras beneath the pines, as the slanting sun shines, the wind shakes the blue mist while flowing springs wind around. The rare treasures within the inner chambers merely dazzle; their light has no [substance].
The method of permeating leakage is numinous and wondrous; who manages or inherits this ready-made livelihood? On the solitary peak, beneath the moon, one hears a clear whistling cry.
Master Bao.

Coming and going along the road beneath Dulungang, with a staff and a hanging cord as my only belongings; past events and future matters are as clear as if seen before one’s eyes. This is no cryptic prophecy;
you must know that in a single thought there is neither past nor present. I laugh long at Old Xiao and his many sufferings from illness;

within this laughter, both medicine and poison are like wolves and tigers. This single wax candle is not a formal entrustment. I jest with you for a moment: when the heat comes, take off your clothes!
Born in trousers.
Where Master Liang lectures, heavenly flowers follow his jade whisk; the moon in the heart of the waves—how could anyone grasp it? An old teacher from a neighboring house stealthily points toward it.
Commentary: He turns his head to look; the void suddenly speaks. Returning to address his disciples, he recounts it again: "My former understanding has all deceived you.
Across the shore lies a mountain shrouded in evening rain. He turns away; amidst a thousand crags and ten thousand gullies, there is no place to be found.
Xiangyan tried to satisfy his hunger with painted cakes; people laughed at you. Yiyuan returned to sweep the valley of Nanyang; only when the bamboo struck and made a sound did he awaken.
Turning slowly to look back, the original face has no place to hide. Yet he looked toward Mount Miao to spread his sitting mat—O, Master!
The horns are fully revealed. Cherish this grace, which exceeds that of one's parents. You must realize it:
a majestic and profound phrase beyond sound. Danxia.
Not fearing the slippery path of stones, returning home, he refuses to be trampled by colts. Under these words, his hundred limbs are all cast away; there is no dharma remaining.
Spiritually resonant, day and night his light penetrates everywhere. In the ancient temple, the weather is cold and the malady flares up again.

At night, he burns the wooden Buddhas all together. Lying across his back to bask in the warmth, he is truly happy. He brushes it aside with a reckless stroke; let the head monk of the monastery be without [a word].
Beard and Hair.
Newly Compiled Record of the Forest (Concluded).
